title: TanStack Charts Introduced with a Framework Agnostic Grammar of Graphics for TypeScript
gist: TanStack Charts launched as a framework-agnostic 'grammar of graphics' charting library for TypeScript, already at roughly 160,000 weekly downloads while still in Alpha and explicitly not production-ready; its creator states almost all of the implementation was written by AI coding agents under his supervision.

insights.claim: A new TypeScript charting library abandons the fixed catalogue of chart components in favour of composing marks, scales, channels, transforms and layers, reviving Leland Wilkinson's grammar of graphics tradition.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Composability rather than chart-type menus is becoming the default abstraction for dataviz tooling, which raises the switching cost away from component-catalogue libraries.
insights.quote: Rather than shipping a fixed catalogue of chart components

insights.claim: The runtime is an independent implementation whose marks-and-channels API is closest to Observable Plot, positioning it as a competitor in the same conceptual lineage rather than a wrapper.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Observable Plot is the nearest incumbent whose mindshare is directly at risk.

insights.claim: Inferred types stay connected to the source row so each mark reads directly from the data shape, making type safety, not rendering, the library's differentiating feature.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: The competitive axis in front-end dataviz has shifted from rendering performance to developer-experience and type ergonomics.
insights.quote: A defining detail is that inferred types stay connected to the source row

insights.claim: A single chart definition renders through adapters for React, Preact, Vue, Solid, Svelte, Angular, Lit and a vanilla DOM host, on the server or in the browser, from one package install (pnpm add @tanstack/charts).
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Framework-agnostic cores let one library capture demand across the whole JavaScript ecosystem instead of fighting per-framework incumbents individually.

insights.claim: React Native remains the acknowledged weak spot of the charting ecosystem, with users calling the state of RN chart libraries 'abysmal' and the maintainer offering only an experimental adapter.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Mobile cross-platform charting is an unserved niche that whoever solves it first can own.
insights.quote: React Native support please! The state of chart libraries in RN is abysmal

insights.claim: The maintainer confirmed an experimental React Native adapter already exists in the documentation, signalling intent to extend the adapter model to mobile.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Adapter breadth is the roadmap, suggesting further encroachment on niche charting vendors.
insights.quote: We have an experimental RN adapter. Give it a try! It’s in the docs.

insights.claim: The creator states on the project's GitHub page that 'almost all of the implementation was produced with AI coding agents under my direct supervision', then reviewed and accepted into the project.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: A widely-adopted library being predominantly agent-written, with humans acting as reviewers, is a live proof point that AI agents can ship real infrastructure-grade OSS.
insights.quote: almost all of the implementation was produced with AI coding agents under my direct supervision

insights.claim: The supervise-and-accept model, where a human maintainer reviews agent output rather than writing it, is implicitly presented as a viable production workflow for a library depended on by millions of applications.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Maintainer leverage, not headcount, may become the constraint on how fast open source ecosystems expand.

insights.claim: A basic React line chart from the library weighs about 29 kB minified and gzipped, with the controlled suite at roughly 38 to 45 KiB.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Concrete payload numbers are the main purchasing argument in front-end tooling.

insights.claim: On the project's own comparison, rival bundles run roughly 45 to 58 KiB for Chart.js, 83 to 92 KiB for Observable Plot, 153 to 173 KiB for Apache ECharts, and far larger for AG Charts.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: The heaviest incumbents, including commercial AG Charts, are the most exposed to a lightweight type-safe challenger.

insights.claim: Commercial competitor SciChart argues the new library is 'often better suited for simpler chart creations that don't require huge, complex data sets to be processed in real-time', steering heavy real-time workloads toward hardware-accelerated renderers.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: The high-end real-time visualization segment looks defensible for commercial GPU-accelerated vendors even as the commodity tier gets eaten.
insights.quote: often better suited for simpler chart creations that don't require huge, complex data sets to be processed in real-time

insights.claim: The project's own large-data guide concedes the same limitation, noting that Canvas removes SVG DOM cost but not scale, guide, or scene compilation work.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Rendering backend swaps do not eliminate the algorithmic cost of large datasets, so real-time analytics buyers still need specialist tools.
insights.quote: Canvas removes SVG DOM cost but not scale, guide, or scene compilation work

insights.claim: A library pulling roughly 160,000 weekly downloads is still officially in Alpha, with the repository warning it is not ready for production and the stability guide advising pinning an exact version.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Download velocity is running far ahead of stated stability, a pattern that creates future migration and support demand.
insights.quote: is not a stable API promise

insights.claim: The Alpha milestone shipped with 11 releases, 188 examples, a full shadcn chart catalog, multiple axes, polar scales and drillable sunbursts, an unusually deep feature surface for a pre-stable release.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Feature depth at Alpha compresses the usual window incumbents have to respond.

insights.claim: The launch was amplified by YouTube walkthroughs such as 'TanStack Did It Again... They Fixed Charts', showing that developer-tool distribution now runs through creator content as much as documentation.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Community media velocity is a leading indicator of dev-tool adoption curves.

insights.claim: The library extends an existing headless, type-safe family spanning Query, Table, Router, Form and the Start framework that is already depended on across millions of applications, and is MIT licensed and free.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Distribution through an established OSS family is the cheapest customer-acquisition channel in developer tooling, and it is aimed at a segment where commercial charting vendors charge money.
